problem_addressed: In 2007 Croatia's own account in the screening report was that EU migrant workers faced in principle the same work permit conditions as third-country nationals, with limited relief for key staff and permits granted outside the annual quota. The Commission found that important adjustments were needed, mainly on non-discrimination against EU migrant workers, including that EU citizens should need no work permit and should not face nationality discrimination in access to employment. The permit elements also belong to RI-FMW-002 and are relied on here because they were the starting point of the reform.
reform_or_mechanism: The Aliens Act in Official Gazette NN 130/2011, passed on 28 October 2011, gives EEA nationals with a right of residence equal rights with Croatian nationals and lets them work without a stay and work permit (Article 153). Article 78(5) relieves EU nationals of the conditions of that article before accession, and Article 236 lets the Government keep earlier rules for nationals of Member States that restrict Croatian workers. Earlier planned amendments to the Act on Foreigners and to the Act on Employment Mediation are recorded in 2007, but their adoption is not stated.
how_implemented: The Act took effect in two steps: it entered into force on 1 January 2012, but Articles 153 to 203 enter into force only on accession, and the Article 78(5) relief ceases on accession. The Commission said Croatia largely fulfilled the requirements on access to the labour market in 2011 and had completed alignment in 2012; these are ratings of legal alignment, and neither names this Act. The only applied step after accession in the evidence is a Commission statement in 2015 that Croatia requires a work permit from nationals of restricting Member States (an RI-FMW-002 element). No source shows the EU workers chapter being used.
evidence_of_results: No outcome evidence found. The items from all eight Croatian sources were searched for data or findings on EU workers' access to jobs in Croatia, or their treatment there, after accession, and none exists. The 2012 alignment finding is a legal rating made before accession, not a result.
limitations_of_evidence: The evidence dates from 2007 to 2015 under logged exception LIM-0027, apart from 2023 civil service texts that belong to RI-FMW-003 and are context only. The Commission never says which law closed the gap, and the source does not say whether the 2011 amendments it mentions under Chapter 23 are NN 130/2011. The Act is machine translated (capped at Medium), the OG 74/13 text is an unofficial free excerpt of Articles 1 to 4, and later amendments were not checked. Items in the unmatched queue on Croatian workers moving to other Member States are not used (G5b), and no Croatian item addresses private sector posts reserved for nationals.
practical_lesson_for_north_macedonia: North Macedonia's stated position is a foreigners law that makes no distinction for EU citizens, with a requirement that runs to the time of accession and further amendments of unknown content. Croatia shows that a general foreigners law can carry a separate regime for EU nationals, adopted before accession and commencing on accession, and that the Commission recorded completed alignment the next year. It does not show that this design earned the rating or that EU workers then had equal access, and it says nothing on reserved private sector posts.
transferable: The underlying mechanism is a legal one: write equal treatment and work without a permit into the law for EU nationals, and tie commencement to accession. It answers the same mechanism as North Macedonia's gap (MEC-01), and North Macedonia's law is within government control and was amended in 2021 and 2025.
not_transferable: Croatia's Act was passed with its accession treaty in view and the source ties it to that treaty, while North Macedonia is at an earlier stage, with its screening report dated 2025. Croatia carried the reform in one Aliens Act, while North Macedonia has a separate law on employment of foreigners. Reciprocity against restricting Member States depended on Croatia's Act of Accession, and no such terms exist for North Macedonia in the evidence. The evidence gives no measure of size or of EU worker numbers with which to compare the two countries.
can_be_attributed: The legal content of the EU provisions, and the timing of their commencement, can be attributed to NN 130/2011 because the text states them. The reciprocal work permit requirement can be attributed to Croatia's own decision because the Commission says so.
cannot_be_attributed: The 2011 and 2012 alignment ratings cannot be attributed to NN 130/2011 or to any named law, because no source makes the connection. Nothing about EU workers' actual access or treatment can be attributed to the reform, because no such evidence exists. The evidence cannot show that commencement on accession was necessary or that it was what the Commission accepted.
description: Croatia wrote equal treatment and permit-free work for EU nationals into its 2011 Aliens Act, commencing on accession, and the Commission recorded completed legal alignment in 2012. There is no evidence of what happened to EU workers in practice.

problem_addressed: The Commission recorded no legislative developments on access to the labour market in its 2024 and 2025 reports and recommended finalising legislative alignment. In 2025 it reported early preparations for amendments that would revoke work and other restrictions for EU citizens. These items do not describe the restrictions in detail.
reform_or_mechanism: The Law on amendments to the Law on Foreigners, adopted on 31 December 2025, places the rules on EU nationals in a separate regime (Articles 150 to 178b). New Article 178a gives EU nationals the right to employment under the same conditions as Montenegrin nationals, and Article 152 gives a right to reside for work. Article 78(1)(7v) carves EU nationals out, which a law firm note reads as the annual quota exemption (an RI-FMW-002 element; the unamended Article 78 was not read).
how_implemented: Under new Article 221b the quota exemption and the other listed articles apply only from accession, so those clauses cannot have been applied yet. Article 221b does not list Articles 150 to 178b, and whether Article 178a applies now or from accession depends on Article 221 of the base law, which was not read. Secondary acts are due within 12 months of entry into force, and none is in the evidence. The EU reports that Chapter 2 was provisionally closed on 15 June 2026, the Government says this confirmed fulfilment of the closing benchmark, and the Government reports 638 residence and work permits to EU citizens from April to August 2026 (an RI-FMW-002 item).
evidence_of_results: No outcome evidence found. The items from all twelve Montenegrin sources were searched for data or findings on EU workers' access or treatment under the new law, and none exists. The clauses deferred to accession cannot yet have results, and for the other clauses the timing is unknown. Provisional closure is a negotiating step and the permit count is a government figure, so neither is an outcome.
limitations_of_evidence: What closed the benchmark is known only from public statements (LIM-0028): the EU common position was not used, the EU release does not say why the chapter closed, and the Government's statement does not say what the benchmark required. No source links the law to the closure, and no Commission assessment of the law is in the evidence. The law is machine translated (capped at Medium), the base law was not read, the law firm note omits the accession clause, and the government annex is proposal text that conflicts on the venue. The closure is provisional and the EU may return to the chapter; public posts are RI-FMW-003 and are context only.
practical_lesson_for_north_macedonia: North Macedonia has the same stated barrier in its foreigners law, and is told to exclude EU citizens from annual quotas and to ensure unrestricted access by accession. Montenegro shows a neighbouring country writing an equal-treatment clause and a quota carve-out into its foreigners law, with at least the carve-out deferred to accession, about six months before the chapter closed. The sequence is suggestive only: it does not show that this law met the benchmark, that deferral was accepted, or that anything changed for EU workers.
transferable: The drafting mechanism is transferable in principle: a separate regime for EU nationals inside the foreigners law, with named clauses tied to accession. The quota element addresses a requirement stated for North Macedonia in nearly the same terms, though the validated position there is that the evidence shows no benchmark under this issue.
not_transferable: Montenegro's closing benchmark and common position set terms that are not public and may not apply to North Macedonia, which is at an earlier negotiating stage. Montenegro uses one Law on Foreigners, while North Macedonia has a separate law on employment of foreigners. Whether Montenegro's deferral would be accepted elsewhere cannot be judged from the evidence, and the evidence gives no comparable measure of size.
can_be_attributed: The text of the equal-treatment clause and the quota carve-out, and the deferral of the clauses named in Article 221b, can be attributed to the 2025 law because the law states them.
cannot_be_attributed: The provisional closure cannot be attributed to the law: the two events follow in sequence, and no source connects them. The 638 permits cannot be attributed to the law or read as showing its failure, because the source does not relate them. No source says the 2025 preparations became this law, and no effect on EU workers can be attributed to it.
description: Montenegro adopted a separate regime for EU nationals in its foreigners law in December 2025, with named clauses applying only from accession, and Chapter 2 was provisionally closed in June 2026. What closed the benchmark is not public, and there are no results yet.

problem_addressed: In 2015 the Commission found Serbian law not yet in line with the acquis, mainly on non-discrimination against EU migrant workers, and said that by accession EU citizens must not need a work permit. In 2024 and 2025 it found the framework partially aligned because EU citizens are covered by the rules for third-country nationals, which is close to its wording on North Macedonia. In 2025 it recommended that Serbia start preparing for alignment.
reform_or_mechanism: By Serbia's own account in 2015, the 2014 Law on Employment of Foreigners provides free access for EU citizens and their family members, entering into force on accession. Amendments in 2017 and 2018, and in July 2023, simplified permit procedures for foreigners generally; the 2023 act sets out a single permit and a labour market test, and it has no separate rule for EU citizens. The Labour Law also prohibits discrimination on grounds of nationality, by Serbia's account. The evidence shows no reform since 2014 aimed at the treatment of EU workers.
how_implemented: The 2023 act applied from 1 February 2024; the Commission said in 2024 that the new system had yet to be fully operational and in 2025 that the procedure had been simplified. The Commission reports work permits issued to EU citizens in both years, 2 071 in 2023 and 526 in 2024, so they remain within the permit regime (RI-FMW-002 items). No source says whether the deferred free-access clause still stands, because the consolidated law was blocked.
evidence_of_results: No outcome evidence found on access or treatment for EU workers. The items from all eight Serbian sources were searched, and the only stated effect is the Commission's statement that the permit procedure was simplified, for foreigners generally and with no processing data, which is treated here as implementation. The permit counts are not outcomes: totals fall from 50 397 to 17 251, the reports do not explain why, and no source links them to a reform.
limitations_of_evidence: What stalled is clear from the Commission's wording, but no source says why alignment on EU workers has not moved. The 2015 report relays Serbia's account and describes the 2014 law, and the consolidated text (SRB-GOV-2023-003) is inaccessible, so only the 2023 amending act was read, machine translated and capped at Medium. The amending act's silence on EU citizens does not show that the base law is silent. No Serbian item addresses private sector posts reserved for nationals, and citizenship conditions for public posts are context only (RI-FMW-003).
practical_lesson_for_north_macedonia: Serbia is a stalled case with the same gap in nearly the same words. It supports the narrow point that amending the foreigners law to simplify permits for all foreigners can earn a chapter-level finding of limited progress from the Commission while the gap it names remains, which is relevant to North Macedonia's own amendments to the same type of law. Serbia also reported a general ban on nationality discrimination in the same report that found misalignment, as North Macedonia does now in its own account. It cannot show why the gap persisted or whether a clause deferred to accession is enough.
transferable: The negative point is transferable: simplifying permit procedures does not by itself address the difference in treatment that the Commission names, because EU citizens stay inside the foreigner regime. This holds only as far as the Commission's wording supports it, since no source states it as a lesson.
not_transferable: Serbia's negotiating position and the reasons for its slow pace are not in the evidence on this issue, so they cannot be compared with North Macedonia's. Serbia's permit reforms were aimed at foreigners generally, so they say little about how to draft rules for EU workers. Serbia's 2015 screening is a decade older than North Macedonia's 2025 screening, and the evidence gives no comparable measure of size.
can_be_attributed: The simplification of the permit procedure can be attributed to the single permit system to the extent that the Commission says so, for foreigners generally. The legal content of the 2023 amending act can be attributed to that act.
cannot_be_attributed: The fall in permits to EU citizens between 2023 and 2024 cannot be attributed to any reform, since the reports do not explain the change. The continuing gap cannot be attributed to any stated cause, because no source gives one. The Commission's partial alignment rating cannot be attributed to any named clause, or to the presence or absence of the deferred clause.
description: Serbia reported a clause giving EU citizens free access on accession in 2014 and later simplified permits for all foreigners, but the Commission still says EU citizens are covered by the rules for third-country nationals. This is a stalled case, and no source says why.
